title: Bolt Grades Explained: 8.8 vs 10.9 vs 12.9
excerpt: What those two numbers stamped on a bolt head actually mean, and how to pick the right property class for the job instead of guessing.
coverAlt: Carriage bolt and hex bolt, an example of a graded fastener

body.text: Pick up almost any metric bolt and you'll find a small marking stamped into the head — something like 8.8, 10.9, or 12.9. That's the property class, and it tells you a lot about how the bolt will behave under load before you ever tighten it down. Mixing up grades, or assuming "a bolt is a bolt," is one of the most common and most avoidable mistakes in fastener selection.
What the numbers actually mean

Under ISO 898-1, the property class marking is read as two numbers separated by a dot. The first number, multiplied by 100, gives you the approximate minimum tensile strength in megapascals — so an 8.8 bolt has a tensile strength around 800 MPa, and a 10.9 bolt around 1000 MPa. The second number is the yield-to-tensile ratio expressed as a fraction of ten — the point at which the bolt begins to permanently deform relative to its ultimate breaking strength. Multiply the two together (roughly) and you get the approximate yield strength as a fraction of the tensile figure.
Grade 8.8 — the everyday workhorse

Grade 8.8 is the most widely used structural and general-purpose bolt grade. It offers a good balance of strength, ductility, and cost, which is why you'll find it everywhere from automotive assembly to general steel fabrication and machinery. If a job doesn't call out a specific higher grade, 8.8 is very often the right default.
Grade 10.9 — higher strength, still weldable-adjacent applications

Step up to 10.9 and you get noticeably higher tensile and yield strength, which lets engineers specify a smaller bolt for the same load, or the same size bolt for a higher load. It's common in structural steel connections, heavy machinery, and anywhere the design has been engineered around the higher strength margin. 10.9 bolts are less ductile than 8.8, so they're less forgiving of over-tightening or shock loading beyond their design limits.
Grade 12.9 — the high-strength specialist

12.9 is the highest property class in common industrial use, offering the greatest tensile strength of the three. It's popular in precision machinery, tooling, and high-stress mechanical assemblies. One important caveat: many structural codes explicitly exclude 12.9 (and higher) from structural steel bolted connections, partly because of increased susceptibility to hydrogen embrittlement, especially if the bolt has been electroplated. Always check the governing code or engineering spec before substituting a higher grade than what's called for — higher isn't automatically better.
How to choose

items: Start with the design drawing or engineering spec — the grade is usually specified for a reason, not a suggestion.
Match the grade of nuts and washers to the bolt; a high-grade bolt paired with a low-grade nut can fail at the nut instead.
Consider the environment — plating and coating choices interact with grade, particularly around embrittlement risk on higher grades.
Never upgrade a specified grade without checking the code — a stronger bolt is not always a safer bolt in a given connection design.

title: 304 vs 316 Stainless Steel Fasteners: Which Grade Do You Need?
excerpt: The one-element difference between 304 and 316 stainless, and why it matters the moment your fasteners get near salt water.

body.text: 304 and 316 are both austenitic stainless steels, and side by side they can look identical — same silvery finish, same magnetic behaviour, same general strength range. The difference that actually matters is chemical, and it shows up the moment either one spends real time near salt water or aggressive chemicals.
The core difference: molybdenum

316 stainless contains roughly 2–3% molybdenum, which 304 doesn't have. That single alloying addition significantly improves resistance to pitting and crevice corrosion caused by chlorides — the kind of attack you get from salt spray, seawater, de-icing salts, or chlorinated washdown environments. It's why 316 is often labelled "marine grade" while 304 is sometimes called "food grade" or "18/8" stainless.
When 304 is genuinely enough

For indoor use, general fabrication, food-contact equipment, and most dry or mildly humid environments, 304 offers excellent corrosion resistance at a lower cost than 316. There's no benefit to over-specifying 316 for an application that will never see chloride exposure — it just adds cost and, in some sizes, longer lead times.
When you should insist on 316

items: Marine and offshore hardware — deck fittings, rigging components, anything exposed to sea spray or immersion.
Coastal construction and outdoor structures within reach of salt-laden air.
Chemical processing, pharmaceutical, and washdown-heavy environments.
Swimming pool and chlorinated water equipment.

body.text: A practical note on mixing grades

Avoid pairing 304 and 316 fasteners in the same assembly where possible, and especially avoid mixing stainless with plain or galvanized carbon steel in a wet environment — dissimilar metals in contact can accelerate galvanic corrosion of the less noble material. When in doubt on a marine or coastal job, specify 316 throughout.

title: G70 vs G80 Chain: Don't Use the Wrong One for Lifting
excerpt: Grade 70 and Grade 80 chain look similar on a shelf. Only one of them is designed and certified for overhead lifting — here's how to tell them apart.
coverAlt: G80 grade connecting link for lifting chain

body.text: Chain grade determines what a length of chain is actually rated and certified to do — and Grade 70 and Grade 80 are two of the most commonly confused grades on a busy job site, precisely because they can look similar at a glance. Getting this wrong isn't a minor spec mismatch; it's a direct safety issue.
What "grade" means for chain

The grade number reflects the minimum tensile strength of the steel the chain is made from, along with the manufacturing and testing standard it's produced and proof-tested to. Higher grade generally means higher strength for a given chain diameter — but grade also determines what the chain is legally and practically approved for.
Grade 70 — transport chain

Grade 70 (sometimes called transport chain) is manufactured and heat-treated for load securement — tying down cargo on trucks and trailers. It's strong, widely available, and cost-effective for that job. What it is not designed, tested, or certified for is overhead lifting.
Grade 80 — lifting chain

Grade 80 is alloy steel chain manufactured specifically for overhead lifting and rigging, proof-tested to lifting standards, and typically supplied with matching Grade 80 hooks, links, and connecting hardware from the same certified system. When you see chain slings on a crane or hoist, this is the grade (or higher) doing the work.
Why the two should never be mixed up

Using Grade 70 transport chain for an overhead lift is a serious safety hazard: it hasn't been manufactured or proof-tested to lifting standards, and its actual behaviour under a dynamic overhead load is not something you can safely infer from its tie-down rating. The reverse mistake — over-specifying Grade 80 for simple tie-down duty — isn't dangerous, just unnecessarily expensive.

items: Always match chain, hooks, shackles, and connecting links from the same grade and, ideally, the same manufacturer's certified system.
Check for the grade marking stamped or embossed on the chain link itself before use.
Keep lifting chain's inspection and certification records on file, and take chain out of service if it fails visual inspection.
When a job involves overhead lifting, specify lifting-rated (G80 or higher) hardware — never transport chain.

title: How to Choose the Right Shackle for Marine Rigging
excerpt: Bow or D-shackle, screw pin or bolt-type, galvanized or 316 stainless — a practical rundown of the decisions that actually matter.
coverAlt: D-shackle, bolt type, used in marine rigging

body.text: Shackles look simple — a U-shaped body and a removable pin — but the specific type, pin style, material, and rating you choose all matter once real load and real seawater are involved. Here's what to actually think about before you order.
Bow shackles vs D (dee) shackles

Bow shackles have a wider, more rounded body, which lets them accept multiple sling legs or load from an angle without side-loading the pin — a common choice for general lifting and rigging where the pull direction isn't perfectly straight. D-shackles (sometimes called chain shackles) have a narrower, more rectangular body built for higher-strength inline pulls, where the load stays aligned with the shackle's long axis.
Screw pin, bolt-type, or safety pin

Screw pin shackles are quick to connect and disconnect by hand, which makes them convenient for temporary rigging — but the pin can work loose under vibration or repeated motion if it isn't checked. Bolt-type shackles use a nut and cotter pin (or a safety pin variant) to positively lock the pin in place, which is why they're the preferred choice for permanent, safety-critical, or vibration-prone lifting applications where a pin backing out simply isn't an option.
Material and finish

Hot-dip galvanized carbon steel is the standard, cost-effective choice for general marine and rigging use, offering solid corrosion protection for most environments. For applications with sustained saltwater exposure, or where corrosion resistance and appearance both matter, 316 stainless steel shackles are the better long-term choice — see our guide to 304 vs 316 stainless for why the grade matters near seawater.
Sizing and working load

items: Always size the shackle to the rated working load of the application — never estimate.
Match the pin diameter to the rope, chain, or sling it will carry; an undersized pin creates a pinch point and uneven load bearing.
Check the size and rating markings forged into the shackle body before installation.
Inspect for wear, deformation, or thread damage on the pin before every use, and retire any shackle that shows cracking or significant wear.

title: DIN, ISO and ANSI Fastener Standards Explained
excerpt: Three letters stamped on a spec sheet can decide whether a bolt actually fits. A quick guide to what each standards body covers.

body.text: Order the "wrong standard" of an otherwise correct-looking bolt, and it may simply not thread into the nut you already have — or worse, it fits poorly enough to fail quietly under load. Fastener standards exist to make sure a part ordered from one supplier behaves identically to the same part ordered from another. Here's what the three letters you'll see most often actually mean.
DIN — Deutsches Institut für Normung

DIN is the German national standards body, and DIN fastener numbers (DIN 933 for hex bolts, DIN 934 for hex nuts, DIN 125 for flat washers, and many more) became the de facto industrial reference across Europe and much of the world during the 20th century. Many DIN fastener standards have since been formally superseded by their ISO equivalents, but the DIN numbers are still so widely used in catalogues and on drawings that they remain the everyday shorthand in the trade.
ISO — International Organization for Standardization

ISO standards exist to harmonize national standards into a single international reference, and for metric fasteners, ISO specifications are now the global baseline — often numerically and dimensionally identical, or very close, to the DIN standard they replaced. When a modern spec sheet calls out an ISO number instead of a DIN number for a common part, it's usually referencing the same geometry under its current, internationally recognized designation.
ANSI / ASME — the American standard

ANSI and ASME standards govern inch-based (imperial) fasteners, which use entirely different thread series — UNC (coarse) and UNF (fine) — from the metric threads used in DIN and ISO standards. A UNC bolt will not thread into a metric nut, no matter how close the diameters look. Equipment sourced from, or built to, North American specifications will typically call for ANSI/ASME hardware.
Why it matters when you're ordering

items: Metric (DIN/ISO) and imperial (ANSI/ASME) fasteners are not interchangeable — always confirm which system your equipment uses.
A DIN and its ISO-equivalent successor are usually interchangeable, but always confirm dimensions on critical or safety-related connections.
Keep replacement parts consistent with the original standard the equipment was built to, especially for threaded connections under load.
When in doubt, quote the full designation (e.g. DIN 933 M12 x 40, Grade 8.8) rather than a generic description.

title: Hose Clips and Clamps: Types, Materials and Where to Use Each
excerpt: Worm-drive or T-bolt, mild steel or full stainless — matching the clamp to the hose and the environment it lives in.

body.text: A hose clamp is one of the simplest parts in an installation, right up until the wrong one lets go under pressure or vibration. Choosing between the common types comes down to clamping force, hose diameter, and how corrosive the environment is.
Worm-drive (Jubilee-type) clips

The classic adjustable band-and-screw clip, tightened with a flathead screwdriver or nut driver. It's inexpensive, widely available, and suitable for the vast majority of low-to-medium pressure hose connections — coolant lines, general plumbing, and light industrial hose runs.
T-bolt clamps

T-bolt clamps use a trunnion and bridge design that applies more even clamping force around the full circumference of the hose, and they hold torque better under vibration than a worm-drive clip. They're the standard choice for larger-diameter hose, higher-pressure connections, and turbo or intercooler piping where a worm-drive clip's point-loading can deform the hose.
Material: mild steel vs full stainless

Zinc-plated mild steel clamps are a cost-effective choice for dry, indoor, low-corrosion environments. Full 304 or 316 stainless steel clamps — band, screw, and housing all in stainless, not just the band — are worth the extra cost anywhere the clamp will see moisture, washdown, marine exposure, or outdoor weathering; a stainless band paired with a plated steel screw housing will still corrode at the housing.
Sizing tips

items: Choose a clamp whose adjustment range comfortably overlaps your hose's outer diameter — don't run a clamp at the very end of its range.
Wider bands distribute clamping force more evenly and resist cutting into soft hose material.
For safety-critical or high-pressure lines, prefer T-bolt clamps over worm-drive.
On marine or outdoor installations, specify full stainless rather than just a stainless band.
